sections.text: Threads are one way to wait for several things at once. Async is another. It suits programs that spend most of their time waiting, such as a web server with thousands of connections. An async fn does not run when you call it. It gives back a future: a value that stands for work that is not finished yet. Nothing happens until something drives the future to completion.

Inside an async fn you write .await after another future. It means: "wait here until this finishes, and let other work run in the meantime". You can only use .await inside async code. Futures are lazy: if you never await or run one, its code never runs.

Rust's standard library defines what a future is (the Future trait) but includes no runtime to run them. Real programs add a crate like tokio for that. This app can't use crates, so the program below carries a tiny runner called block_on, built only from std. It asks the future "are you done?" (that is called polling). If the answer is "not yet", it parks the thread until the future says it is ready to be asked again. Read the helper only if you are curious. It also contains PauseOnce, a small future that answers "not ready yet" the first time it is asked, so that you can watch an .await pause.

Look at the order of the lines in the Output comment at the end of the code. Calling greet("Ada") printed nothing. All the work happened inside block_on. The .await on PauseOnce paused greet once and then it continued, while add(2, 3).await finished at once. Note that block_on runs just one future, so no two futures make progress together here. Interleaving needs a runtime or a join helper.

You can read async fn as a function that returns a future. async fn add(a: i32, b: i32) -> i32 gives back something that will produce an i32 once it has run. .await is how you get that i32 out. If you forget .await, you hold the unfinished work, not the number.

A runtime like tokio can run thousands of futures on a few threads: when one future waits, the runtime switches to another. This is where .await really pays off. With tokio you put #[tokio::main] above your async main function, start tasks with tokio::spawn, and run futures side by side with tokio::join!. The snippet below shows an async fn using it. When should you use async and when threads? Threads are simple and good for heavy computation. Async is for programs with many tasks that mostly wait, especially network code. Many projects use both.

Coming from JavaScript or C#: a JavaScript Promise, or the Task a C# async method returns, is already running by the time you get it. A Rust future does not: it is lazy and does nothing until awaited or polled (a Python coroutine is lazy in the same way). Rust also ships no executor, so you choose one (tokio is the most common; smol is a small alternative). If you know Python's asyncio, async fn is like async def, and block_on plays the role of asyncio.run.

exercise.prompt: run() calls add_one once. Make it call add_one a second time on the result, with .await, and return that. The program should print: 3

quiz.question: What does calling an async fn give you?
options: The final result straight away, after the whole body has run
A future: a value standing for work that has not run yet
A new operating-system thread that has already started the body

quiz.question: What does .await do?
options: Waits for that future to finish, letting other work run in the meantime
Starts a new operating-system thread to run the future in parallel with main
Converts the future into its output type without ever having to wait

quiz.question: Why do real async programs add a crate like tokio?
options: Rust has no async keyword, so a crate must add the syntax itself
async functions can't call println! unless a crate wraps it for them
The standard library defines futures but has no runtime to run them
